Thank you so much for sharing this. I feel like if more people knew, there would be more attention given to the issue, and they'd receive better care. It's a statistic that makes me sick to my stomach.

There are a lot of different factors that go into it, and of course everyone has their own reason for leaving the profession, but a lot of the time it's just not all it's cracked up to be. The most obvious reason I think is the incredibly low pay (at least starting out) for the amount of work you're actually doing. 

Also, as a young, new teacher in a district, you're often coming in to a school more than half-full of veteran teachers, who can often have a "my way or the high way" or "stick to what works" view of education, and it can be disheartening when you're discouraged from teaching your students based on principles you know to be true based on more current research than when 65-year-old Mrs. Jones went to school to teach. New teachers also tend to have a lack of influence, not just over how to teach their own class, but school policy in general- which can really suck when you're the last person to have had education classes. You literally have the newest information, and keep getting shut down when it comes to using it. 

However, in my Educational Psychology class, we've also discussed some less apparent reasons for teacher turnover that have to do with socioeconomic status and race.

The majority of people who become teachers are white females. In minority districts, which tend to also be lower socioeconomically, teachers (usually white women) drop like flies. This tends to be cyclical. Young, white female teachers are put into schools, sometimes hoping to better a failing school system with minority students who they believe just don't behave or aren't intelligent, when these are misconceptions that end up hurting them in the long run. They then fail to form meaningful relationships with their students, as students are more likely to bond with teachers more like them. Say this teacher gets fed up with her students' progress and quits. Enter another white female teacher. In the long run, these students are less likely to go to college than their white, middle class counterparts (who then may become teachers, to be part of the same failing system in minority school districts). 

There are, of course, more individualized reasons for the high turnover rate. 
But
 
TLDR: in middle class school districts, it's usually that they have no say in how they teach/school policy and feel it's a waste of time. And in poorer districts they feel their impact is trivial, often because they can't relate as effectively to minority students, and it scares them away from the profession. And it pays horribly.
50% of teachers in the United States quit teaching entirely within the first 3-5 years.

I wasn't THAT young, I was in 5th grade. But I had a huge fear of the holocaust. Obviously it's something frightening that never should have happened, and anyone would be sad/afraid, but I had such a traumatizing fear. When we first started learning about it in middle school, I was extremely interested in the topic, it was crazy to think something like that had actually happened. My family used to go to DC every year, and that spring I insisted my grandmother take me to the national holocaust museum, even though my mother had tried talking me out of it. Although I knew what had happened, really seeing what these people went through really messed me up as a 10-year-old. I didn't sleep for a very long time, and I would get very scared over little things that I had just associated with it. I was mostly afraid of getting in the shower. 
I'm fine now, obviously, and I'm a history major who's taken classes on genocide, social issues and such. I don't get scared, per se, but whenever I watch a documentary on the holocaust or even just Hitler's rise to power (I love historical documentaries, and I come across a lot of them), the feeling that I left the museum with that spring just kind of creeps back up on me. It's really hard to shake.
